opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I keep coming back to.

When we started SGLang, the name itself said a lot about where our heads were: it began as a *structured generation language*. The idea was that people weren't just sending one prompt and getting one answer anymore. They were writing programs around language models: multiple calls, branching, constrained outputs like JSON, tool use, and agents that loop. We wanted a way to express those programs naturally and then have the runtime execute them very efficiently underneath. Things like RadixAttention, which reuses KV cache across calls that share prefixes, came directly out of that thinking. If you know the structure of the program, you can optimize it.

Over time, much of the community's energy went into the runtime side, the serving engine. That's because the most urgent pain point in industry was simply making models fast and cheap to serve at scale. I think that was the right thing to focus on. But I don't think it's the end state.

Ultimately, I see SGLang as a layer that lets people describe *what* they want an AI system to do, at the level of intent and structure, while the system figures out *how* to do it efficiently. It's a bit like the evolution of databases. People write SQL declaratively, and the query optimizer handles execution. For AI, the "query" is increasingly an agentic workflow. It has many model calls, tools, memory, retries, and multiple models working together. The interface should let you express that cleanly, and the engine should co-design scheduling, caching, and hardware use around it.

There are a few directions I care about:

First, **agents as first-class workloads.** Today's serving systems still largely think in terms of individual requests. But real applications are long-running, stateful sessions. The interface needs to understand sessions, shared context, and the dependencies between steps, so we can do much smarter cache management and scheduling.

Second, **reliability and controllability.** Structured outputs were an early example. People need guarantees: this output will parse, this agent will follow this protocol, this call stays within this budget. A good interface between people and AI gives you knobs that actually mean something.

Third, **openness.** I really believe this layer should be open source and community-driven. It's becoming critical infrastructure. You don't want the way humans interact with AI systems to be locked inside one company's black box. With SGLang, we've had contributors from academia, startups, and big companies all over the world, and that diversity is exactly what keeps it honest and moving fast.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: I hope SGLang evolves from "a fast way to serve models" into "the natural way to program AI systems," where expressing what you want is simple, and efficiency comes for free underneath.

r001.rationale: The response says the community’s energy shifted to the runtime because the urgent industry need was serving models quickly and cheaply at scale.

r002.rationale: It proposes that SGLang evolve into “the natural way to program AI systems,” letting people express their intent and workflows through an interface.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't want SGLang to be "the interface between people and AI" in the sense most people mean it. When we started it, the name was Structured Generation Language, and the original idea was a programming model: you should be able to write a multi-step LLM program with control flow, parallel calls, constrained decoding, and have the system execute it efficiently. That's still the right layering, I think. People talk to models through chat windows, agents, IDEs, voice, whatever product wins. SGLang's job is to sit underneath that and make whatever they're doing fast and cheap and correct, so the application layer gets to be creative instead of fighting the serving stack.

So if I describe where it should go, it's a few directions. The first is that the boundary between "frontend language" and "runtime" should keep collapsing. The reason RadixAttention and prefix caching mattered is that once you can see the structure of the program, you can schedule it much better than if you just get a stream of independent requests. As workloads become agentic, with long shared contexts, tool calls, branching, tens of thousands of tokens of system prompt reused across millions of calls, that structure is where all the performance is. The engine should understand sessions, not just requests.

The second is that it has to stay genuinely open and hardware-neutral. I care a lot about SGLang being something a lab in a university, a startup with two GPUs, and a large company with a few thousand can all run, and contribute back to. If the interface to AI ends up controlled by a handful of closed serving stacks, that's bad for the whole ecosystem. Open models are only as useful as the open infrastructure to run them.

And the third one, which is more about people than technology: I'd like SGLang to make the cost of experimentation go to zero. A lot of what we think of as "model capability" is really inference-time behavior, how you decode, how you sample, how you structure the reasoning. Those should be things a grad student can try on a Tuesday afternoon, not something only a frontier lab can afford. If we get there, then SGLang's role as an interface isn't that users touch it directly, it's that it quietly determines how much of the AI around them is possible to build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses runtime efficiency and serving challenges, but does not explain that growing backend inference challenges shifted SGLang’s development effort toward runtime optimization.

r002.rationale: The response says SGLang should remain an underlying programming model and runtime, with people interacting through product interfaces; it does not propose SGLang itself as the language people use to interact with AI.

astra-6.text:
I think SGLang should ultimately let people express what they want an AI application to do without having to manage all the complexity of how it runs. You should be able to describe the workflow—how the model interacts with tools, how different steps connect—and let the system handle execution efficiently.

There are really two parts to that: an interface that gives developers enough control to build richer applications, and a runtime that makes those applications fast and economical. Ideally, those evolve together. As interactions with AI become more complex, the interface should remain simple, while the system underneath does more of the work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a runtime that runs applications fast and economically, but it does not say backend inference challenges have become more prominent or that this shifted SGLang’s development effort toward runtime optimization.

r002.rationale: The response describes an interface for expressing workflows and building applications, but does not propose that SGLang should take the form of a language for people to interact with AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think SGLang should ultimately let people express what they want an AI system to do without having to manage all the complexity underneath. You should be able to describe a workflow, bring together different models and tools, and have the system execute it efficiently.

That means the interface and the runtime need to evolve together. A more expressive interface gives people room to build richer applications, while an efficient runtime makes those applications practical. Ideally, developers can focus on the behavior they want, and SGLang handles more of the execution details. That’s the direction I’d like to see: making increasingly capable AI systems easier to program and use.
